fields.mechanism: Passive internal lattice scaffold (mesh) integrated into the catheter lumen to maintain lumen geometry and prevent occlusion, mirroring the structural support provided by a stent mesh pore.
fields.intervention: Design the multi‑lumen drainage catheter with an embedded self‑expanding metal or polymer lattice that lines the floor lumen, creating a permanent internal conduit that resists collapse and biofilm buildup without increasing outer diameter.
fields.expected_effect: Sustained drain conductance; reduced lumen occlusion risk; flow restored even if external lumen narrows; no increase in catheter outer size.
fields.falsification_test: Compare occlusion rates in a bench‑top flow loop using standard catheters versus catheters with internal lattice under identical proteinaceous slurry; measure flow decline over 72 h—hypothesis falsified if lattice catheters show no statistically significant improvement.

fields.mechanism: Using a stent mesh pore to route a drainage catheter through a flared self‑expanding metal stent, thereby enlarging the effective lumen for flow without increasing external diameter.
fields.intervention: Integrate a thin‑walled, flared self‑expanding metal scaffold into the multi‑lumen catheter wall, with a pre‑formed ≥4 mm mesh aperture that allows the inner drainage lumen to extend through the scaffold, creating a larger internal flow channel while keeping the outer catheter diameter unchanged.
fields.expected_effect: The enlarged internal flow channel reduces hydraulic resistance and resists occlusion, maintaining drain conductance over time without increasing the catheter’s outer diameter.
fields.falsification_test: Bench‑test paired catheters (standard vs. scaffold‑integrated) under identical viscous fluid and particulate conditions; measure flow rate decline and time to occlusion—significant improvement in the scaffold‑integrated design would confirm the mechanism.

fields.mechanism: Radial expansion of a self‑expanding metal stent maintains lumen geometry while a catheter placed through the stent mesh provides a low‑resistance fluidic pathway for drainage.
fields.intervention: Integrate a thin, self‑expanding metal mesh ring inside each lumen of the multi‑lumen drainage catheter that expands to prop open the lumen, and thread the catheter tip through the mesh to create a combined stent‑catheter conduit without increasing outer diameter.
fields.expected_effect: The internal mesh prevents lumen collapse and occlusion by tissue or debris, preserving drain conductance and allowing sustained flow through each lumen.
fields.falsification_test: In a bench‑top model simulating viscous secretions, compare flow rates over 7 days between catheters with the internal expandable mesh and standard catheters; a significant loss of flow in the control but not in the mesh‑enhanced catheter falsifies the mechanism.

fields.mechanism: A self‑expanding metal stent mesh provides a rigid scaffold with a pore that supports a catheter lumen, preventing collapse and occlusion while the catheter passes through the mesh without increasing its outer diameter.
fields.intervention: Integrate a flared self‑expanding metal mesh sleeve around the floor lumen of the multi‑lumen drainage catheter, creating a ≥4 mm mesh aperture through which the floor lumen is threaded, thereby forming a catheter‑mesh complex that maintains patency without enlarging the catheter’s external diameter.
fields.expected_effect: Restored drain conductance and reduced lumen occlusion under physiological and compressive conditions, while preserving the original outer diameter of the catheter.
fields.falsification_test: Conduct an in‑vitro flow‑through test comparing standard multi‑lumen catheters to catheters equipped with the mesh‑supported floor lumen under simulated peristaltic compression and proteinaceous fouling; measure flow rate decline over 72 hours to determine if the mesh‑supported design maintains ≥90 % of initial flow.
